One plastic tea bag can release billions of microplastic particles into a single cup.

The silky pyramid bags are usually nylon or PET. Even paper bags are often heat sealed with polypropylene around the edge, so the shape tells you nothing.

The fix is unusually cheap: loose leaf and a steel infuser takes plastic out of the brewing path entirely, and it normally works out cheaper per cup than bags.

Full guide to which brands are actually plastic free, link in bio.

Polyester is plastic, and every wash sheds hundreds of thousands of microplastic fibres.

The part most people miss is where they go. Those fibres end up in indoor air and house dust as much as in waterways, which is how you end up breathing them.

Washing cold, running fuller loads and washing less often all reduce shedding measurably. A filter bag catches a good share of the rest. None of it requires replacing your wardrobe.

Microwave safe is a melting standard, not a health one.

It means the container will not warp. It says nothing about what leaches into your food when you heat it, and heat is exactly what drives leaching.

Borosilicate and tempered soda lime glass are both genuinely microwave safe and sidestep the question entirely. Look for glass containers with glass lids, not plastic ones.

Bottled water averages roughly 240,000 plastic particles per litre.

The detail that matters more than the number: most of them are nanoplastics. That is the fraction small enough to cross into tissue, and also the fraction almost no filter is tested against.

PET sheds into its own contents, and heat during shipping and storage makes it worse. A hot truck is part of the story.

The kimchi headlines got it backwards.

That study tested one isolated bacterial strain in germ free mice, not kimchi the food. It bound polystyrene nanoplastics in a dish, which is a very long way from eating kimchi and clearing plastic from your body.

Watch for the chemical for particle swap. Lowers BPA or reduces PFAS quietly becomes removes microplastics, and those are completely different claims.

The part of chewing gum that never gets smaller is a plastic polymer.

It comes from the same family used in glue and industrial coatings, and it hides behind a single ingredient line reading gum base. That one term can cover dozens of synthetic polymers, none of which have to be named.

Chicle is the original gum base: tree sap, not polymer. A few brands still use it and say so plainly on the pack.

BPA free does not mean safe.

Manufacturers removed BPA and dropped in BPS and BPF, which are structurally similar and show comparable hormonal activity in lab studies. The label changed. The chemistry barely did.

It is a textbook regrettable substitution: swap a chemical people have heard of for one they have not, and keep the reassuring claim on the front of the pack.

Skip the claim and check the material instead. Full guide, link in bio.

#bpafree #bps #microplastics #plasticfree #endocrinedisruptors #nontoxicliving #cleanliving #plasticpollution

Certification has not caught up to the particles that matter most.

NSF 401 certifies a filter against microplastics. There is no equivalent standard for nanoplastics, which is the size that actually crosses membranes.

Reverse osmosis works around this because it filters by pore size. The membrane does not care what the particle is called, so it captures well below the certified range. Physics rather than paperwork.
